verses.text: It is doubtless not profitable for me to boast. For I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord.
I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago (whether in the body, I don’t know, or whether out of the body, I don’t know; God knows), such a one caught up into the third heaven.
I know such a man (whether in the body, or outside of the body, I don’t know; God knows),
how he was caught up into Paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.
For if I would desire to boast, I will not be foolish; for I will speak the truth. But I refrain, so that no man may think more of me than that which he sees in me, or hears from me.

By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively.
Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me.
He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.
Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.
I have become foolish in boasting. You compelled me, for I ought to have been commended by you, for in nothing was I inferior to the very best apostles, though I am nothing.
Truly the signs of an apostle were worked among you in all perseverance, in signs and wonders and mighty works.
For what is there in which you were made inferior to the rest of the assemblies, unless it is that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong.

Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you; for I seek not your possessions, but you. For the children ought not to save up for the parents, but the parents for the children.
I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less?
But be it so, I did not myself burden you. But, being crafty, I caught you with deception.
Did I take advantage of you by anyone of them whom I have sent to you?
I exhorted Titus, and I sent the brother with him. Did Titus take any advantage of you? Didn’t we walk in the same spirit? Didn’t we walk in the same steps?
Again, do you think that we are excusing ourselves to you? In the sight of God we speak in Christ. But all things, beloved, are for your edifying.

For I am afraid that by any means, when I come, I might find you not the way I want to, and that I might be found by you as you don’t desire; that by any means there would be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, factions, slander, whisperings, proud thoughts, riots;

that again when I come my God would humble me before you, and I would mourn for many of those who have sinned before now, and not repented of the uncleanness and sexual immorality and lustfulness which they committed.

footnotes.content: Paul sets us on guard right away. He knows the temptation—to trumpet our own victories, our spiritual experiences, our moments of encounter with the divine. But he catches himself. True strength isn't in saying 'look what happened to me.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fourteen years—and he's only now telling this? The man caught up into Paradise keeps his counsel. What moves Paul to speak isn't pride, but the Corinthians' need. Notice his uncertainty about his own body—the veil between the seen and unseen world is thin, and mysteries remain mysteries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul repeats his wonderment: Was he in the body or out? He won't pretend to know what only God knows. This humility—this refusal to claim what he cannot be certain of—is the true hallmark of an apostle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paradise—the place of blessing beyond all telling. Yet even the apostle cannot speak what he heard. Some words belong only to God and the soul that heard them. There is wisdom in silence, in knowing when words fail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the hinge: Paul will boast only on behalf of 'such a one'—this man who caught glimpses of Paradise. His own boasting? Only in weaknesses. The trick of the enemy is to make us proud of our own strength. Jesus teaches the opposite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul could speak truth about himself—he has earned the right. But he chooses restraint. 'Let no one think more of me than they can see and hear.' What maturity, what mercy, to refuse the temptation of exaggeration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thorn in the flesh—a messenger of Satan, yet God permits it. Sometimes the Lord allows our weakness to be exposed and painful, not as punishment, but as a schoolmaster. Pride is more dangerous than a thorn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three times Paul begs the Lord to remove it. Not a once-and-done prayer, but persistent, honest, human crying. The Lord does not always remove the thorn. What He does is something better—He answers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' How many tears have been dried by these words? How many stumbling saints have risen again on this promise? Not removal of the thorn—resurrection through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul moves from prayer to thanksgiving. He takes pleasure—actual pleasure—in weakness, injury, distress. Not in self-pity, but in the way these teach him to trust. When he cannot lean on himself, he leans wholly on Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Corinthians have pushed Paul to this uncomfortable boasting. He speaks of his apostolic standing—but only because the flock needs assurance. Even then, 'I am nothing.' This is not false modesty; it is the gospel lived.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Signs and wonders, mighty works—the marks of an apostle. Paul does not deny them. But notice: they are signs of his calling, not of his merit. The vessel is nothing; the grace working through it is everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul turns the tables gently—and with irony. The only 'wrong' he did to the Corinthians was not to burden them with his own needs. His love has been expressed in self-restraint. 'Forgive me this wrong'—the saints pick up the irony and smile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks as a father—the third visit awaits, and still he will not burden them. The saying about children and parents, not laying up treasure for the next generation, was a custom of the ancient world; Paul echoes it to show his love is not mercenary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Spend and be spent. Paul's life is an offering. 'If I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less?' The parent knows the paradox: the more we pour out for our children, the less we may receive in return. And we love them anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul addresses a false charge—that he somehow tricked the Corinthians. He denies it firmly. A leader's integrity is not a luxury; it is necessary. When suspicion enters, the gospel loses ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul names no names—only asks: did any of the companions I sent take advantage of you? Let the record speak. A good leader invites examination and is willing to stand in the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Titus and the brother walked with him in the same spirit, the same steps. Partnership in the gospel means walking together in character. When emissaries carry your heart, they must carry your integrity too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul returns to his central plea: We are not excusing ourselves to you, but speaking in Christ, before God. Everything Paul does is for the building up of the flock. His defense is not self-defense; it is self-giving.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The catalog of fears—strife, jealousy, anger, factions, slander. When Paul lists such things, we hear not judgment but the ache of a shepherd's heart. He has seen these weeds grow where the gospel should flourish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this: that leaders come not to lord it over the flock, but to mourn with those who mourn, to weep over sin, to grieve the lost opportunity for repentance. We live still in this tension between the call to apostolic authority and the call to humble love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
